text: Investigation: Burning and Suppression of Solids Acronym: BASS Official PSI title: Burning and Suppression of Solids(BASS) Investigation type: Microgravity Investigation Research area: Combustion Science Sub-research area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Fuel phase: solid Fire safety topics: prevention; suppression; modeling Flight platform: International Space Station (ISS) PSI keywords: Flame Spread; Fire suppression system; Damkohler number; Boundary layer; Fire safety; Forced Flow Flame; Kinetic regime

Objective: Bridge the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity (PSI listing) ; examine burning and extinction of solid fuels, N2 suppression

Hypothesis: Materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity at identical pressure, O2 concentration and temperature; testing all but the thinnest materials needs longer microgravity time than drop towers or parabolic aircraft give.

Fuel / samples: Fabric 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass by mass (SIBAL in table), Nomex, Ultem, PMMA (spheres 1 and 2 cm, slabs), paraffin and Japan-wax candles, wax slabs (experiment table) Hardware / facility: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ISS; flow duct; Kanthal wire (29 gauge) igniter

Test conditions: Airflow up to 40 cm/s (page), concurrent and opposed flow; flow duct 76 x 76 mm; spheres and cylinders also used; fact sheet: co-flow 5-50 cm/s, N2 suppressant, ISS air ~21% O2 at 1 atm. Per-run conditions are NOT in the experiment table (only date, test and sample numbers, material).

PSI approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) meas...

Measurements: Video and still images; anemometer; radiometer; flame shape; spread rate; time to extinction; Kanthal wire (29 gauge) igniter at one end of the fabric (PSI listing) Key findings: Guide: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative - materials can burn at lower O2 in microgravity than in 1-g; local suppressant jet can entrain air and sustain or strengthen the flame | Publication abstracts and NASA technical reports read 2026-11-15: findings are in insights.csv (rows with this psi_id and evidence_type publication_abstract).

Space benefits: NASA materials selection rests on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (1-g behaviour only, no low-gravity effects); results feed first-order models of heat release in spacecraft fires and extend NASA cone calorimeter (Test 2) data to performance-based material selection; N2 as suppressant links to current and planned extinguishment techniques; results guide ground-based research and validate combustion models, supporting safety of future crewed missions. Earth benefits: Validated detailed combustion models can be extended to normal-gravity flames and wide terrestrial combustion problems.

text: Investigation: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Acronym: SAME Official PSI title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment(SAME) Investigation type: Microgravity Investigation Research area: Combustion Science Sub-research area: Spacecraft Fire Safety Fuel phase: solid (smoke from overheated materials) Fire safety topics: detection Flight platform: International Space Station (ISS) PSI keywords: Smoke; Surface Combustion; Fire Safety; Bio-Astronautics; Smoldering

Objective: Quantify the sizes that liquid smoke particles reach in low gravity and relate the droplet size distribution to smoke generation and transport conditions; develop a numerical code predicting smoke-droplet growth from pyrolysis rate, vapour properties and flow (PSI page). Fact sheet: evaluate ionization (Shuttle) and photoelectric (ISS) smoke detectors in microgravity.

Hypothesis: Without strong buoyant flow, smoke from a pyrolysing or smouldering source grows (nucleation, condensation, coagulation) into larger particles than in 1-g, helped by higher vapour concentration and longer residence time near the source; liquid-aerosol smokes should show much larger droplets and lower number density, which changes smoke-detector response and may leave some detectors silent.

Fuel / samples: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, lampwick (cellulose) and dibutyl phthalate (DBP); the experiment table gives four conditions for Teflon and 'same conditions' for the other four (fact sheet: 30 samples, 6 per material) Hardware / facility: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ISS: near-field hardware inside the glovebox with a Far Field Box attached; two smoke detectors; thermophoretic samplers; video cameras. PSI hardware field cites the Comparative Soot Diagnostic hardware report (Expedition 15 per fact sheet)

Test conditions: Table: air flow 5 or 10 cm/s; weight-loss rate 1 or 2 mg/min; smoke aging 1 or 20 min. Page: heater on for 15-60 s, each event about 2 min; sample temperature, flow field and aging time controlled; 1-g runs later matched to the flight mass-loss rates

PSI approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the tw...

Measurements: Smoke-detector responses (transcribed from the video record); thermophoretic samples for TEM (primary and aggregate particle dimensions); sample mass loss; 59 analysed-data spreadsheets (228 MB) and a final science report (3.7 MB) in the repository Key findings: PSI page states goals and hypotheses only. Fact sheet: significant mass in particles larger than 1 micron; Teflon smoke mostly below 1 micron; all samples produce sub-micron particles best seen by ionization detectors; light scattering works well for most cases; detection should target pre-fire heating products rather than soot. The SAME-R page adds that the SAME TEM grids came back contaminated and unusable.

Space benefits: Reduced-gravity baseline data on detector sensitivity to smoke, against which current and future detection technology can be judged; technology for an advanced fire detector for long-duration spacecraft. Earth benefits: Smoke detectors for other extreme enclosed environments such as submarines or underwater laboratories.

(Page: the SAME hypotheses apply unchanged to the reflight.)

Fuel / samples: Kapton (29 table rows), silicone rubber (22), lampwick (20), Pyrell intumescent fire-retardant foam (20; replaced DBP), Teflon (18) Hardware / facility: SAME hardware in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), ISS; new GRC-built M-pass instrument replaced one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures (DustTrak + ionization detector); thermal precipitator for TEM

Test conditions: Table (109 rows, 42 of them aged-smoke 'a' rows): inlet velocity 0-8.1 cm/s (8.1 for 74 rows, 0 for 22), heater resistance ratio Rt/R0 1.22-1.48, heating 60 s typical, net aging time tens of seconds to >800 s; flight tests 16 Jul - 9 Sep 2010 (66 test points per page); higher heating temperatures and no-flow heating added

PSI approach: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell(R), an intumescent fire-retardant f...

Measurements: Aerosol moment instruments (number, diameter, mass), ionization and photoelectric detector signals, TEM samples; three post-flight ground tests to validate the log-normal size-distribution assumption behind the moment method; 86 analysed-data files (495 MB), 223 raw files (5.7 GB), final report (4.6 MB) Key findings: PSI page gives no results; the table lists test conditions only (no measured sizes). Fact sheet: moment-based size statistics compared with SMPS and TEM; focus on pyrolysis products rather than soot.

Space benefits: Together with SAME: quantitative data on detector sensitivity to reduced-gravity smoke and a baseline for an advanced fire detector for long-duration spacecraft. Earth benefits: Smoke detectors for submarines, underwater laboratories and similar environments.

Objective: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity; measure effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He, SF6 named on page); develop predictive models of combustion limits; obtain high-resolution droplet burning rate, extinction, radiation, soot and temperature data (PSI page)

Hypothesis: Microgravity fundamentally alters combustion and extinction of liquid fuel droplets (no buoyant convection changes species and energy transport, radiative loss and kinetics), so flammability limits and suppressant efficacy differ from normal gravity.
Fuel / samples: Methanol (157 runs) and heptane (117 runs) droplets (experiment table) Hardware / facility: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

Test conditions: Pressure 0.5-1.5 atm for LOI tests (page); table: 0.69-3.05 atm, O2 12-34%, N2 diluent with CO2 or He suppressant up to 0.7 and 0.45 mole fraction; droplet initial diameter ~1-4.7 mm; fuels methanol and heptane; free (drifting) and fiber-supported droplets; slow sub-buoyant flow tests

PSI approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a funct...

Measurements: Droplet diameter vs time, burning rate, visible flame extinction diameter, burn time, test end (extinction / disruption / completion); LOI vs pressure and suppressant (approach) Key findings: Page states objectives and hypothesis, not results. Publications report cool-flame-supported quasi-steady heptane burning and cool-flame extinction (Nayagam et al.), CO2 effects on methanol extinction, support fiber effects - not yet read. | Publication abstracts and NASA technical reports read 2026-11-15: findings are in insights.csv (rows with this psi_id and evidence_type publication_abstract).

Space benefits: Improved fire safety protocols for future missions where traditional suppression may be ineffective; data on CO2, He and SF6 suppressant effectiveness. Earth benefits: Fire safety in confined or reduced-gravity settings (submarines, high-altitude aircraft); more efficient, less toxic suppression systems; cool flames and low-temperature combustion inform engine design (efficiency, emissions).

Objective: Extend FLEX-1 to fuels and ambient conditions closer to real combustors and provide benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion for validating numerical simulations and new theory. Itemised on the page: role of liquid-phase mixing in bi-component droplets; steady and unsteady liquid- and gas-phase phenomena in pure-fuel burning; flame-extinction mechanisms and their boundaries; soot formation (volume fraction, soot-shell dynamics); further items cover convective flow and droplet arrays. Fact sheet adds surrogate fuels and droplet-droplet interaction.

Hypothesis: Droplet-combustion simulations solve the full gas-phase flow but approximate chemistry, radiation and gas-liquid coupling, and those assumptions have never been checked against benchmark data. Microgravity removes buoyancy so the basic processes can be seen directly, including the transition between radiative and diffusive flame extinction; the goal is benchmark bi-component droplet data over a wide range of initial conditions.

Fuel / samples: Planned matrix (experiment table, 8 rows): iso-octane, n-octane, heptane, decane, ethanol, propanol/glycerol 95/5 and 80/20, heptane/iso-octane 50/50; initial droplet diameter 1.5-5 mm; fibre-supported or freely deployed; single droplets and binary linear arrays Hardware / facility: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ISS; retractable hot-wire igniter (1-5 s); droplet translation to impose slow flow

Test conditions: Chamber pressure 0.5-3.0 atm; O2 mole fraction 0.1-0.4 per page text (table: 0.17 / 0.21 / 0.25 / 0.30) in O2/N2 or O2/He; ambient 25 C; flow 0.1-5 cm/s; about 2 min gas settling and at least 10 s dwell before ignition. Independently varied: fuel, ambient gas composition, pressure, initial diameter, translation velocity, spacing and size in a binary array

PSI approach: The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the...

Measurements: High-speed and colour imaging of droplet and flame (burning rate, extinction, soot), chamber pressure and temperature; raw data 10,081 files (1.22 TB) plus 63 calibration files (4.4 GB) Key findings: PSI page gives objectives, approach and expected impact - no results. The experiment table is the planned matrix (fuel x condition ranges), not an as-run log, so there are no per-run outcomes for FLEX-2 in PSI page data. 48 publications are listed (not read).

text: Objective: Explain the large difference in soot formation between 1-g and 0-g flames by deriving temperature and soot-volume-fraction fields from SPICE data in PSI (more than 1,600 raw DSLR images) and by advanced soot modelling; reconcile microgravity and normal-gravity behaviour and identify the processes that control smoke-point development.

metadata.full_name: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets

text: Hypothesis: Microgravity gives longer, more diffuse, cooler and sootier flames than normal gravity; feeding measured temperature fields into the simulations should narrow the gap between measured and predicted soot.

metadata.full_name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

text: Objective: Using FLEX data from PSI, run new simulations and ozone-sensitised counterflow-flame experiments to: (1) build a diagram of the flammability limits of diffusion cool flames under radiation, diffusion and convection; (2) connect the flammability and extinction limits of hot and cool flames; (3) verify phenomena seen in the ISS FLEX tests; (4) obtain extinction-limit, temperature and species data for validating kinetic and radiation models; (5) extend the cool-flame experiments further (text continues on the page).

metadata.full_name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

text: Hypothesis: Asks what makes hot flames turn into cool flames and how the cool-flame flammable region relates to the hot-flame flammability and extinction limits; O2 concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convection are expected to control the transition.

metadata.full_name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

text: Measurements: Cool-flame and hot-flame extinction limits with and without ozone, CH2O PLIF and thermometry, chemiluminescence; 8 data items mapped to publication figures (Analyzed Data workbook, 0.74 MB) Key findings: PSI page (Research Impacts): the warm flame has a double reaction-zone structure and plays a critical part in the transition between cool and hot flames; at elevated pressure the flammable region of warm and cool flames widens because low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity rises with pressure - relevant to engines running at 20-40 atm.

text: Hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, so the time-temperature history of the vapours and the particle trajectories change and the smoke composition changes; the chemistry of the burning material also shapes the smoke.
